name: Amira Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive the water truck round the haul roads at a large mine, keeping dust down so the other drivers can see. I am 58 with a vocational certificate, but I learnt the safe speed on bends from years behind this wheel. The best part is handing over a clear road; twelve hours of jolting with a nearly empty tank is the hard part. My husband repairs bicycles from our garage, our grown children have their own homes, and we have less than a month's expenses put by. I use an AI tool now and then to make sense of a manual, after somebody checks its answer against the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the drivers dust control is still a job, even if the daily forms fill themselves. I would say a checked manual helps, but the road decides how much water I put down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think our thin savings matter more than a small change in forms right now. I also worry a minor software saving could give management another reason to trim cover shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the water truck on its normal rounds and mark slippery bends in the log. I'd put the bicycle repair money toward the electricity arrears whenever my husband has a good week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The work still makes sense to me in this picture. I am uneasy about the electricity bill, because a quiet week in the garage quickly shows up at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with that bill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The electricity bill rose after the old heater failed, and we paid for the replacement first. We have been catching up in small pieces since then, not building a proper reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the road log if the forms get quicker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A driver nearly slid on the west bend after a sudden shower last month. I wrote down the time and surface. The next shift needed my notes on the slippery bend, not just a completed box.

think: I think our **thin savings** matter more than a small change in forms right now.
I also worry a minor software saving could give management another reason to **trim cover shifts**.
do: Keep driving the **water truck** on its normal rounds and mark slippery bends in the log.
Put the **bicycle repair money** toward the electricity arrears whenever my husband has a good week.
feel: I feel **steady at work** but **uneasy** about a bill already behind.
S0.quote: The next shift needed my notes on the slippery bend, not just a completed box.
fieldNote: Her **road judgment** remains central in a modest software change, especially around bends and weather.
The **electricity arrears** and uneven bicycle-repair income already leave the household with little room for another bill.

steps.text: Keep driving water-truck rounds and logging slippery bends
Direct bicycle-repair income to electricity arrears when work comes in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew dispatch screens might change first while dust still needs a truck on the road. I would ask for a demonstration on shift before signing off on a new route plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think tighter routes could take away cover shifts that help us clear the electricity balance. I will try a proven tool, but I will not trust a dry map over what I see through the windscreen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask dispatch to show the new route screen during a paid handover. I'd compare its watering plan with my bend notes for a week before using it. I'd take extra bicycle repairs with my husband if mine hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can get used to a screen if it earns its keep. Losing even a few shifts would be harder than learning where to tap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare on the screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check whether it sends me back to the west bend after a shower and whether the tank can finish the loop. If it misses either point, I would tell dispatch before following it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could the garage take on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can clean and set up bicycles, but my husband does the difficult repairs. We could take one or two more at weekends, not replace a mine wage.

feel: I feel **anxious** about hours and cautiously open to a tested tool.
S1.quote: We could take one or two more at weekends, not replace a mine wage.
fieldNote: She tests **route software** against observed road conditions rather than rejecting it outright.
Her **weekend bicycle work** is a small fallback, and she expects lost cover shifts to hurt household cash.

steps.text: Ask dispatch for a paid demonstration of the route screen
Compare software watering routes with bend notes for a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI in 2028 can run dispatch, but water trucks still need drivers until robots around 2031. I would ask for a written training offer before trusting any promise about replacement jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a robot water truck to threaten my wage around 2031, long before our debts are settled. My husband's garage cannot carry the household, and there are few mine jobs within reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine trainer this month whether road-inspection jobs are being created. I'd enroll in paid road-inspection training if the mine guarantees wages during the course. I'd cut holiday travel and direct that money to the electricity balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because the truck may be taken out from under me while I still need every pay packet. I have a route to ask about, but I cannot make an unpaid course work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2029, after thinking AI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still water the roads if people are driving the trucks, and I would check whether dispatch is giving us fewer hours. Robots in this picture do not arrive until around 2031, but I would not wait until then to ask about inspection work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your husband after that meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my husband exactly whether the mine will pay me to train. We cannot pay a course fee from the bicycle till while the electricity balance is still there.

S2.quote: We cannot pay a course fee from the bicycle till while the electricity balance is still there.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 dispatch change** from the 2031 robot threat to her hands-on job.

steps.text: Ask the mine trainer about paid road-inspection positions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2031 thinking AI gives us time to examine dispatch before robots reach the road around 2034. I would ask the mine to put apprenticeship places beside any plan for automated trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031, I could learn road inspection while I still have wages from driving. A 2034 robot date still worries me because retirement is only a hope with our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the safety lead for a paid shadow shift checking road conditions next quarter. I'd apply for a road-inspection apprenticeship if places open to older drivers. I'd keep the water-truck rounds in 2032 while learning which conditions the sensors miss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is a hard change, but five years gives me time to watch it work before betting our bills on it. I would feel anxious until I saw a paid place with my name on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that shadow shift show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to walk the west bend with the safety lead after rain and see what the sensors report. If road sensors miss loose shoulder gravel, that is a real inspection task I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there are no places for older drivers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep driving while there is paid work and ask the mine association to press for fair entry rules. My children have households of their own, so I would not make them fund my training.

say: I would say **2031 thinking AI** gives us time to examine dispatch before robots reach the road around 2034.
I would ask the mine to put **apprenticeship places** beside any plan for automated trucks.
think: At **63 in 2031**, I could learn road inspection while I still have wages from driving.
A **2034 robot date** still worries me because retirement is only a hope with our savings.
do: Ask the **safety lead** for a paid shadow shift checking road conditions next quarter.
Apply for a **road-inspection apprenticeship** if places open to older drivers.
Keep the **water-truck rounds in 2032** while learning which conditions the sensors miss.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with enough warning to test a paid transition.
S3.quote: If road sensors miss loose shoulder gravel, that is a real inspection task I can do.
fieldNote: She uses **site knowledge** to identify a possible inspection role, with evidence from a wet bend.
Her **apprenticeship application** depends on places for older workers and continued pay, not family support.

steps.text: Ask the safety lead for a paid road-inspection shadow shift
Apply for an inspection apprenticeship if older drivers qualify

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2036 thinking AI may change the office while our water trucks stay driven until roughly 2039. I would tell the crew ten years of warning should mean real training slots, not a farewell speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 in 2036 and may still need wages if the repair business stays uneven. By 71 in 2039, I would hope to stop climbing into the truck, but I cannot assume we can afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid driving shifts while I can do them safely. I'd clear the electricity arrears first, then set aside a fixed amount from each pay packet. I'd review retirement costs with my husband each year, using actual bills and earnings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The longer warning gives me room to put the house in order. Time does not turn a thin account into a pension on its own. That still makes me uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in 2037?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 69, I would still drive if the road is safe and we need the wage, or take paid inspection shifts if that path opens. Dispatch might be run by AI then, but capable road robots are still about two years away in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help you stop working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would help us move furniture or fix a tap, and we would do the same for them. I would not count their wages in our retirement plan; they have their own bills.

say: I would say **2036 thinking AI** may change the office while our water trucks stay driven until roughly 2039.
I would tell the crew **ten years of warning** should mean real training slots, not a farewell speech.
think: I will be **68 in 2036** and may still need wages if the repair business stays uneven.
By **71 in 2039**, I would hope to stop climbing into the truck, but I cannot assume we can afford it.
do: Keep **paid driving shifts** while I can do them safely.
Clear the **electricity arrears** first, then set aside a fixed amount from each pay packet.
Review **retirement costs** with my husband each year, using actual bills and earnings.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about retirement money despite the longer warning.
S4.quote: Time does not turn a thin account into a pension on its own.
fieldNote: She keeps **paid work at 69** in view instead of assuming retirement follows an anniversary.
The **arrears-first plan** fits a household with irregular repair income and no stated pension amount.

steps.text: Keep paid water-truck shifts while driving remains safe
Clear electricity arrears, then save a fixed amount each payday

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because a water-truck robot around 2031 would arrive while we still need my wage. A paid inspection apprenticeship with a real job at the end would help. So would honest notice before the roster changes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: An experienced driver might still be useful where road sensors fail after rain. I wish you had asked where the sensors fail, because the mine needs to listen to the people who know those bends.

headlineQuote: An experienced driver might still be useful where road sensors fail after rain.
portrait: Amira is a **58-year-old water-truck driver** at a large mine, with a vocational certificate and lower pay.
Her husband's uneven bicycle-repair income and **electricity arrears** leave less than one month's expenses saved.
She uses **AI occasionally** and accepts tools after testing them against actual road conditions.
She seeks a **paid inspection apprenticeship** before robot trucks arrive, while keeping retirement tied to bills.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** because water-truck robots around 2031 could take a wage the household needs.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **paid inspection apprenticeship** leading to a real position and clear notice of roster changes.
